item.title: Evening Edition, Friday, October 9, 2026
item.description:
Hurricane Isaias strengthened to a Category 3 major hurricane with 120 mph winds hours before an expected Friday-night landfall on the northern Gulf Coast. The National Hurricane Center's 1 p.m. CDT advisory put the center about 240 miles south of Pensacola earlier in the day, moving north-northeast at 16 mph, with tropical-storm conditions already starting on the coast. Landfall is expected this evening in the warning area, with weakening after landfall.

The International Criminal Court itself was put under U.S. sanctions, blocking its U.S.-linked assets and barring most American dealings with it. Treasury's OFAC added the court to its blocked-persons list Oct. 9 under Executive Order 14203, announced alongside a State Department release. General licenses allow a wind-down through April 7, 2027, and carve out telecom and software services, pensions, and services tied to detainees.

The UAE attorney general said the Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash FZ1073 into Ben Gurion Airport's passenger terminal in a suicide attack. In a statement carried Friday by the UAE state news agency WAM, Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said investigators found the 29-year-old Omani co-pilot had developed a premeditated plot to seize the aircraft and strike the terminal to cause the greatest possible loss of life, and had used two earlier Tel Aviv trips to study the route and airport. He said the suspect confessed in the presence of his lawyer and claimed he acted alone, while investigators keep checking for accomplices or other links. A pilot assigned to the return flight entered the cockpit, restrained the co-pilot with a cabin crew member and passengers, and the crew landed in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Flydubai said it is supporting the investigation. No charges have been announced.

A fully loaded crude supertanker was hit by an unknown projectile off the UAE coast, outside the Strait of Hormuz, UKMTO said. The strike about 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera, UAE, set a fire that was put out; crew status and damage were unknown. Shipping sources named the Panama-flagged GEM NO.2. It follows a tanker strike off Qatar earlier this week.

The Nobel Peace Prize went to Navi Pillay, the South African jurist and former U.N. human rights chief, for promoting peace and international law. The Norwegian Nobel Committee cited her role in ensuring war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted. The prize, worth 12 million Swedish crowns, will be presented in Oslo on Dec. 10.

An ICE officer shot a man in his car with a 5-year-old in the back seat in Manhattan, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani demanded ICE halt city operations. The Dominican man, identified as Oscar Belgal, was wounded in the neck during an arrest Oct. 8 in Marble Hill and is held outside New York state. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officers did not know the child was in the car and criticized the city's sanctuary policies.

item.title: Morning Edition, Friday, October 9, 2026
item.description:
Hurricane Isaias, now packing 100 mph winds, is expected to hit the northern Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday, forecasters said. The National Hurricane Center said Isaias could briefly reach major-hurricane strength early Friday before wind shear weakens it near landfall, most likely near the Alabama-Florida border. A life-threatening storm surge is forecast from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Suwannee, Fla., with hurricane warnings for parts of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi and up to 15 inches of rain in spots.

U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner meet Ukrainian officials in Miami Friday on a new joint proposal to end the war, the White House confirmed. A broader session with national-security advisers from the U.K., France and Germany plus NATO, the EU and U.S. European Command is set for 11:30 a.m. ET. Overnight, Russia launched 136 drones at Ukraine, killing one person in Zaporizhzhia, while Russia said it downed 505 Ukrainian drones over 19 regions.

Durham, N.C., firefighter Andrew Brokes, 24, was killed in a roof collapse while searching a burning home; Gov. Josh Stein ordered flags lowered. Two other firefighters were hurt at the fire on Marly Drive on Oct. 8. Flags fly at half-staff across North Carolina on Oct. 9.

U.S. strikes on Iran will not resume before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, President Trump said, citing "productive discussions" with Tehran. Trump said on Truth Social Thursday that the naval blockade of Iran stays in full force. The post reversed his comments the night before that he was weighing pre-election strikes; Brent crude rose above $104 a barrel Thursday.

Isaias became the Atlantic season's first hurricane, and hurricane warnings now cover the coast from Mississippi to the Florida Panhandle. At 5 a.m. ET Thursday, NOAA Hurricane Hunters put Isaias's top sustained winds at 80 mph, about 420 miles south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River, moving east-northeast at 9 mph. A hurricane warning covers Ocean Springs, Miss., to the Bay/Gulf County line in Florida, and a storm surge warning runs from the mouth of the Mississippi to the Steinhatchee River, with 5 to 7 feet of surge possible from Ocean Springs to Indian Pass and in Mobile Bay. The National Hurricane Center expects 3 to 7 inches of rain, up to 10 in spots, from southeast Louisiana to the Panhandle, and says Isaias should be a strong hurricane by landfall late Friday or early Saturday.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico keep White House access through at least Tuesday after a federal judge extended his order blocking their ban. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly said he will rule by Tuesday on a longer preliminary injunction. The outlets were barred from White House grounds nearly three weeks ago; their lawyer called it viewpoint discrimination.

Microsoft, Adobe and six major IT outsourcing firms were suspended from the Labor Department program employers use to sponsor foreign workers for green cards. Vice President JD Vance announced the move Thursday at a White House Fraud Task Force news conference, citing alleged fraud, and said that for every worker Microsoft laid off it hired "one and a half foreign indentured servants." Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the department is suspending Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini from the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program, the required step before an employer can sponsor a worker, including H-1B visa holders, for a green card, and is suspending Microsoft and Adobe because of multiple active federal investigations. Officials gave no end date. Sonderling also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, will be investigated over allegedly bringing in international students to undercut American wages; Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had been served. Microsoft did not immediately comment.

Oil prices jumped about 4%, with Brent crude near $104 a barrel, on Gulf tanker attacks and Gulf of Mexico shutdowns ahead of Hurricane Isaias. Brent, the international benchmark, rose 3.8% to about $104 a barrel in early Thursday trading. Tanker attacks tied to the Iran war are at their highest of the conflict, and Shell and Chevron said they were shutting in Gulf of Mexico production as Isaias approaches. The 10-year Treasury yield rose 5 basis points to 5.331%, and Japan's Nikkei fell 1.4%. Prices were from early trading and can move during the day.

Houthi attacks on airports in Riyadh and Abha killed three people and wounded 36, Saudi Arabia said; the Saudi-led coalition then struck 82 Houthi targets. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said Abha International Airport and Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were attacked on Oct. 6 and 7; an Egyptian and an Algerian were killed at Abha and a Sudanese national in Riyadh. The Houthis said they fired a ballistic missile at the Riyadh airport, their second claimed attack on it this week; the coalition said that missile was intercepted. The coalition said it then destroyed 82 military targets, including mountain missile sites and command centers, AFP reported.

The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration over $20 million in taxpayer-funded TV ads it calls illegal pro-Trump propaganda. The complaint, filed Wednesday in U.S. District Court in Washington, names President Trump, the White House, Homeland Security and the Office of Management and Budget, and asks the court to declare the ads illegal and stop federal money from paying for them. The ads, marked 'Paid for by the U.S. Government,' began airing in September; $20 million has been drawn from a $175 million DHS immigration-enforcement fund, and more than $12 million had been spent so far, AP reported, citing AdImpact. No ruling yet.

Texas executed Jamaal Howard, the first U.S. execution since Tennessee's failed lethal injection of Christa Pike a week earlier. Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m. CT Wednesday in Huntsville after a dose of pentobarbital, the same drug used on Pike. He was convicted of killing store clerk Vickie Swartout in a 2000 robbery. The Supreme Court denied his requests to stop the execution; only Justice Jackson said she would grant a stay. AP said it was the 30th U.S. execution this year.

Tropical Storm Isaias put the northern Gulf Coast under a hurricane watch, with forecasters warning it could hit as a major hurricane late Friday. The National Hurricane Center's hurricane watch runs from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass on the Florida Panhandle, with a storm surge watch from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Yankeetown, Fla., and tropical storm watches on either side. As of 1 p.m. CDT, Hurricane Hunters found Isaias strengthening, with 50 mph winds about 520 miles south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi, moving east-northeast at 8 mph. NHC director Michael Brennan said it could reach Category 3 before landfall late Friday or early Saturday. Florida declared a state of emergency for more than a third of its counties, and producers shut in a significant share of Gulf offshore oil and gas output, AP reported.

Russia's overnight attack on Ukraine killed at least 30 people, up from 11 this morning, including 19 in a Pryluky apartment building. A Russian cruise missile hit a residential building in Pryluky, Chernihiv region, killing 19 people, five of them children, and injuring 55, Ukraine's emergency service said as rescuers kept searching the rubble. Authorities count at least 30 dead and 138 injured across Ukraine over the past day, including three in Kyiv and two each in Kremenchuk, Kirovohrad and Sumy regions. Ukraine's Air Force said Russia fired ballistic missiles, 48 cruise missiles (39 stopped) and 130 drones (117 stopped).

Russia's overnight missile and drone attack on Ukraine killed at least 11 people, including five in a Pryluky apartment building, Ukraine's president said. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired about 70 missiles, many of them ballistic, plus attack drones at Kyiv and at least 12 regions, with energy infrastructure a key target. A missile hit a five-story apartment building in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region, killing five and injuring 26, including five children. Two people were killed in Kyiv and two in Oleksandriia, and apartment buildings were damaged in Dnipro and Kremenchuk. The attack came on Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday. Separately, Russian officials said they intercepted almost 900 Ukrainian drones overnight.

The tanker Acers was hit by multiple projectiles about 50 nautical miles north of Qatar, with casualties, Britain's UKMTO said. UKMTO said the master reported the strike at about 3 p.m. ET Wednesday, about 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar; it gave no casualty count. Maritime security firm Vanguard Tech identified the ship as the Antigua-flagged, Greek-managed tanker Acers. It is the first reported tanker attack in the western Gulf in weeks, far from the Strait of Hormuz.

Wells Fargo's programs to raise Black homeownership are under a Fair Housing Act investigation by HUD. HUD Secretary Scott Turner announced the probe Oct. 7, and HUD sent a letter to Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf saying it will examine whether the bank offered different products or terms based on race. The programs date to the bank's 2017 pledge of $60 billion in loans to add 250,000 Black homeowners by 2027, expanded in 2022 to refinancing for minority homeowners. Findings could lead to charges or a Justice Department referral; this is an investigation, not a finding.

Fed minutes show most officials expected another interest-rate increase by year-end, according to the September meeting record released Wednesday. At the Sept. 15–16 meeting the FOMC voted 12–0 to raise its target range a quarter point to 3.75%–4%. The minutes say most participants judged another increase would likely be appropriate by year-end and saw inflation risks skewed to the upside, citing energy prices and AI-driven investment. Staff estimated August PCE inflation at 3.8% (core 3.4%) and no longer see inflation returning to 2% until 2029. The next meeting is Oct. 27–28. Earlier Wednesday, Treasury sold $39 billion of 10-year notes at 5.300% with a 2.77 bid-to-cover, stronger than average demand two days after the 10-year yield hit a 2002 high.

An 18-year-old was charged with planning a terror attack on the Mall of America after buying an AK-47 from undercover FBI agents, prosecutors say. Federal prosecutors in Minnesota say Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, a U.S.-born citizen, was arrested Tuesday in a Richfield park after paying $600 for an AK-47 and 200 rounds to an undercover FBI employee posing as an ISIS member. The complaint alleges he told an informant he planned to kill non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24. U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said he spoke of killing 30 to 60 people. He made his first court appearance Wednesday in St. Paul; the charges are allegations.

Social Security identity-theft victims will get a single point of contact at the agency under a law President Trump signed Wednesday. H.R. 5345, the Improving Social Security's Service to Victims of Identity Theft Act, requires the Social Security Administration to give one point of contact to people whose number has been misused or whose card was lost. Trump also signed S. 766, the Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act, which requires a yearly report on federally funded projects more than five years behind schedule or more than $1 billion over budget.

Saudi Arabia launched an air-safety investigation into the Flydubai FZ1073 cockpit attack, separate from the UAE's criminal probe, Reuters reported. Three people close to the matter told Reuters on Wednesday that Saudi Arabia notified aviation agencies abroad it will run a safety investigation under international rules, because the flight was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked the captain with an axe. The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board confirmed it assigned a representative, since the Boeing 737 MAX was built in the United States. Saudi authorities did not comment, and it is unclear whether findings will be published. Israel's Aircraft Safety Investigation Authority said Israel offered to take part but has not been invited. The UAE-led criminal investigation, which its prosecutor general calls a terrorist attack, continues; no charges have been announced.

Optional Practical Training for foreign students would cost $70,000 per student under a Homeland Security proposal filed Wednesday. The ICE proposed rule, filed for public inspection Oct. 7 and set to publish Oct. 8, would charge $70,000 for an F-1 student's first OPT period and $30,000 for each later one; schools would recommend OPT only for students whose fee they pay. DHS says that without the fees it may shut the program down entirely. Comments are due 30 days after publication. It is a proposal, not a final rule.

Imports worth $2,500 or less would face tighter filing and bond rules under a Customs and Border Protection proposal filed Wednesday. The CBP proposed rule, filed for public inspection Oct. 7 and set to publish Oct. 8, would change filing rules for informal entries of $2,500 or less, create a new electronic entry type for mailed packages, require mail carriers to send an extra data element, and require a basic import bond for some informal entries. Comments are due 60 days after publication.

item.description:
Russia's overnight missile and drone attack on Ukraine killed at least 11 people, including five in a Pryluky apartment building, Ukraine's president said. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired about 70 missiles, many of them ballistic, plus attack drones at Kyiv and at least 12 regions, with energy infrastructure a key target. A missile hit a five-story apartment building in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region, killing five and injuring 26, including five children. Two people were killed in Kyiv and two in Oleksandriia, and apartment buildings were damaged in Dnipro and Kremenchuk. The attack came on Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday. Separately, Russian officials said they intercepted almost 900 Ukrainian drones overnight.

Tropical Storm Isaias formed in the western Gulf of Mexico and is forecast to strengthen rapidly before nearing the northern Gulf Coast Friday. As of 4 a.m. CDT Wednesday, the National Hurricane Center put Isaias near 22.0N, 94.1W with maximum sustained winds of about 40 mph, moving east-northeast at 8 mph. Forecasters expect it to become a hurricane by Thursday. Heavy rain, gusty winds, storm surge and possible tornadoes are expected from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect yet.

Yemen's Houthis fired ballistic missiles and drones at Aden's international airport, forcing a Cairo flight to divert, as Saudi Arabia downed a missile near Riyadh. Yemen's government said at least two ballistic missiles and several drones targeted the runway and terminal, with one missile landing near the runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due; the flight was sent to Jeddah and the terminal evacuated. The Houthis said they targeted Saudi military supplies at a nearby camp. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile north of Riyadh. The Houthis also claimed attacks on Saudi airports in Riyadh and Abha. Fighting has intensified as Saudi-backed government forces push toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Drones sank one merchant ship and set another on fire inside Bulgaria's Black Sea economic zone, Bulgaria said; the sunken ship's crew is missing. Sea and air drones hit the two ships about 70 nautical miles east of Byala early Tuesday local time. The Togo-flagged, Turkish-owned Alfa Watan sank and its crew is unaccounted for. The Palau-flagged Able, carrying wheat, caught fire; all 18 crew were rescued and taken to Varna, and one is in critical condition with severe burns. Prime Minister Rumen Radev called the attack "absolutely unacceptable" and said the drones were "clearly either Russian or Ukrainian"; who launched them has not been established. Bulgaria is in contact with NATO, and President Iliana Iotova called a national security council meeting for Wednesday.

Ukraine launched about 650 drones at Moscow overnight, killing two people in one of the largest attacks on the Russian capital in two years, Russian officials said. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said most of the drones were shot down, 105 of them close to the city. Moscow region Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said one person died in Radumlya and one in Barybino, and a drone set a retail warehouse on fire in Litvinovo. Reports put the injured at six to nine. The 650 figure comes from Russian officials; Ukraine has not confirmed it. Russia's Defense Ministry said it struck Ukraine's Black Sea ports of Chornomorsk and Izmail overnight.

The S&P 500 closed at a record high Tuesday, its first since August, as Treasury yields eased from their highest levels since 2002. The S&P 500 rose 44.98 points, or 0.6%, to 7,818.93. The Dow gained 253.38 to 51,521.28, and the Nasdaq rose 122.48 to 27,599.79, its second straight record. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 5.28% from 5.31% late Monday. The S&P 500 is up 23% from its late-March low.

Anduril and the Navy will spend $6.6 billion on a new Baltimore County shipyard to build Virginia-class submarine parts, the White House announced. Anduril is investing $3.7 billion and the Navy committed up to $2.9 billion through a contract for the facility, called Arsenal-2, at Tradepoint Atlantic. Maryland officials said it will create more than 3,100 permanent jobs; initial operations are targeted for 2030. President Trump promoted the project Tuesday.

A federal judge in Boston blocked the Trump administration's policy of fining migrants up to $1.8 million for not leaving the U.S. after final deportation orders. U.S. District Judge George O'Toole stayed the ICE rule used to impose the fines and barred enforcement of fines issued after June 27, 2025, while a class-action lawsuit brought by two fined migrants moves forward, Reuters reported Monday. He found the fines were likely imposed unlawfully, including because ICE skipped public notice and comment and the Department of Homeland Security did not consider individual circumstances. Since last year the administration has levied fines of $998 a day, applied retroactively for up to five years. DHS said in July it had issued more than 100,000 such fines totaling about $84 billion.

Twelve sailors were injured when a projectile hit the tanker On Peace in the Strait of Hormuz, India's foreign ministry said. India said 12 of the Panama-flagged tanker's 19 crew were hurt, 11 of them Indian, and Oman helped evacuate them to Khasab for treatment. India did not say who carried out the attack. The ship appears to be the tanker UKMTO reported hit Monday evening with an engine-room fire, though that has not been formally confirmed.

World oil production will fall about 5 million barrels a day this year because of the Iran war, the Energy Information Administration projected. In its Oct. 6 Short-Term Energy Outlook, EIA projected world petroleum production falling from a record 106.3 million barrels a day in 2025 to 101.1 million in 2026, and world demand falling from 104.4 million to 102.4 million. The G7 agreed Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves.

Cornell's trustees hired former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to lead an independent review of the 2024 Chi Phi assault case. A new Special Committee of Cornell's Board of Trustees said Tuesday that Yates, a partner at King & Spalding, will review how the university prevents and responds to sexual assault and misconduct, including campus police, hearings and discipline, coordination with prosecutors, and oversight of fraternities and sororities. Her team will also examine Cornell's response to the October 2024 allegations by Jane Doe against Chi Phi members, including whether it followed its own policies. Yates will report to the committee, and the board said it intends to share the findings with the Cornell community. The state attorney general's separate criminal investigation continues; no criminal charges have been filed.

The 2018 Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods will stay in place after U.S. industries asked for them to continue, the U.S. Trade Representative said. USTR's notice, "Continuation of Actions: China's Acts, Policies, and Practices Related to Technology Transfer, Intellectual Property, and Innovation" (FR Doc. 2026-20510), went on Federal Register public inspection Tuesday and publishes Oct. 7. It comes out of the second four-year review of the tariffs, which began in May. A companion notice (2026-20511) makes conforming changes to product exclusions.

A Nigerian Air Force transport plane crashed in Ondo State, killing all 25 people aboard, the Air Force said. The ATR-42, NAF 931, was on a routine flight from Benin City to Lagos when it went down at Igbokoda on Oct. 5. It carried five crew and 20 passengers. On Tuesday the Air Force confirmed there were no survivors, released the victims' names and ordered an investigation.

Russia told the WHO no plague case has been recorded in Irkutsk and that the dead lab worker's contacts tested negative; about 60% have left quarantine. WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier read Russia's official reply at a Geneva briefing Tuesday: "No case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk," and tests of everyone identified as a contact were negative for dangerous pathogens, Reuters reported. Rospotrebnadzor again said testing found no microorganisms linked to the 28-year-old Anti-Plague Institute technician's work, and a Shelekhov district official said about 60% of those quarantined have been released. Russia's reply did not say whether plague was ruled out in the worker herself, whom officials say died Oct. 2 of pneumonia of unknown cause. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Russia should share more information and that Washington is watching "hour by hour"; the WHO still rates the risk to the general public as low.

item.description:

Kenya confirmed its first imported Ebola case, a Kenyan citizen who traveled from Congo through Uganda and died in Nairobi. Health Minister Aden Duale said Tuesday the patient arrived in Kenya on Saturday and was isolated and treated at Nairobi Hospital before dying.

Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan's execution by firing squad was approved by President Trump; the U.S. military has not executed anyone since 1961. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on X that the Army secretary will set the time and place. Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was sentenced to death for the 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, that killed 13 people.

A tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was hit by an unknown projectile Monday evening, starting an engine-room fire, the UK maritime agency UKMTO said. UKMTO cited the ship's captain and said there were no early reports of injuries. It is the third tanker struck in two days, after a crude tanker Saturday and an oil tanker and an LNG tanker Sunday. Iran's Fars news agency said Iran had acted against 13 vessels in the past seven days. Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guards turned an inbound tanker back on Monday.

A Trump executive order lets off-road dyed diesel be used on highways through Dec. 31 and moves to defer the federal diesel excise tax. The order, "Emergency Tax Relief on Diesel Fuel," was signed Oct. 5. Treasury has five days to decide whether disaster-style relief applies; if it does, federal diesel excise tax payments are deferred for fuel used Oct. 5 through Dec. 31. The IRS must also announce within five days that it will not penalize selling or using dyed diesel on highways in that period. The White House says the deferral carries no interest or penalties and that Europe agreed to release 100 million barrels of refined diesel from its reserves over four months.

The Supreme Court opened its new term by turning away hundreds of appeals, including Second Amendment, COVID vaccine-mandate and "Let's Go Brandon" cases. Monday's order list from the justices' Sept. 28 long conference denied review in United States v. Hembree, leaving in place a 5th Circuit ruling that the federal felon-in-possession gun ban was unconstitutional as applied to a man whose prior felony was meth possession. The Court also denied two challenges to Washington state COVID-19 vaccine mandates (Petersen v. Snohomish Regional Fire and Rescue; Roberts v. Ferguson) and left in place a 6th Circuit ruling letting a Michigan school bar "Let's Go Brandon" sweatshirts. In Mullin v. National TPS Alliance, it sent the Venezuelan and Haitian Temporary Protected Status case back to the 9th Circuit in light of its June ruling in Mullin v. Doe, and it asked the Solicitor General for views in three mortgage-escrow interest cases. The Court heard its first argument of the term, Suncor Energy v. Boulder County, on whether federal law bars state climate-damage suits against oil companies.

Treasury warned foreign banks still doing business with Iran's financial sector that they can be sanctioned at any time, without advance notice. The OFAC alert, dated Oct. 5 under "Operation Economic Outcast," tells banks dealing with sanctioned Iranian banks to end those ties right away and says serving Iranian banks or their branches abroad now carries sanctions risk. OFAC also amended an Iran FAQ on restricting a foreign bank's U.S. correspondent accounts. Earlier steps include cutting Banque Misr UAE's U.S. correspondent access in August and sanctioning Turkey's Golden Global Bank and Russia's VTB Bank in September.

The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.31% Monday, its highest level since 2002. The benchmark yield rose 3.4 basis points on the day, Dow Jones Market Data reported, extending a selloff that pushed it to a 19-year high in late September. Big tech shares still lifted stocks, and the euro fell to a 17-month low against the dollar on worries about France's debt. U.S. crude for November fell 1.84% to settle at $89.43 a barrel. The 10-year yield is a benchmark for mortgage and other long-term loan rates.

Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces retook Dhubab and other towns near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait from the Houthis, Yemeni officials said. The offensive, called "Yemen Dawn," also took the towns of Bab and Hadeid, according to officials and witnesses. Saudi coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said 100 fighter jets are supporting the push. A U.S. official and a regional official told AP the United States provided intelligence sharing, targeting and planning help. Government leaders say the goal is to retake Sanaa. The WHO says the fighting has killed at least 959 people.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards forced an inbound tanker to turn back in the Strait of Hormuz, as a third tanker in two days was hit by a projectile. UK Maritime Trade Operations said Monday the IRGC hailed the tanker 11 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, and told it to turn back or be targeted; the master complied. Separately, UKMTO said another tanker in the strait was struck by an unknown projectile that set its engine room on fire; the crew was fighting the blaze and no casualties or environmental damage were reported. Iran's parliament speaker said the strait stays closed until seven U.S. conditions are met, and President Pezeshkian called talks with Washington meaningless. Pezeshkian on Sunday accepted the resignation of Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad as exports dried up under the U.S. blockade.

item.description:
The Supreme Court opened its new term by turning away hundreds of appeals, including Second Amendment, COVID vaccine-mandate and "Let's Go Brandon" cases. Monday's order list from the justices' Sept. 28 long conference denied review in United States v. Hembree, leaving in place a 5th Circuit ruling that the federal felon-in-possession gun ban was unconstitutional as applied to a man whose prior felony was meth possession. The Court also denied two challenges to Washington state COVID-19 vaccine mandates (Petersen v. Snohomish Regional Fire and Rescue; Roberts v. Ferguson) and left in place a 6th Circuit ruling letting a Michigan school bar "Let's Go Brandon" sweatshirts. In Mullin v. National TPS Alliance, it sent the Venezuelan and Haitian Temporary Protected Status case back to the 9th Circuit in light of its June ruling in Mullin v. Doe, and it asked the Solicitor General for views in three mortgage-escrow interest cases. The Court heard its first argument of the term, Suncor Energy v. Boulder County, on whether federal law bars state climate-damage suits against oil companies.

The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.31% Monday, its highest level since 2002. The benchmark yield rose 3.4 basis points on the day, Dow Jones Market Data reported, extending a selloff that pushed it to a 19-year high in late September. Big tech shares still lifted stocks, and the euro fell to a 17-month low against the dollar on worries about France's debt. U.S. crude for November fell 1.84% to settle at $89.43 a barrel. Federal price-transparency rules finalized Monday require health insurers to give cost estimates by phone and post standardized price files. The two passengers on the lost Bermuda–Boston air ambulance were named as a Bermuda mother and son; all six aboard are presumed dead. The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as a storm approached. A Florida school bus carrying 37 students flipped in a Winter Haven crash Monday, killing a 10th-grade girl and a Jeep occupant. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said an oncoming car crossed the center line shortly after 6 a.m. and hit the side of the bus bound for Winter Haven High School, tearing off a tire and sending the bus head-on into a Jeep that caught fire. item.title: Morning Edition, Monday, October 5, 2026
item.description:
Brazil's first-round count has Flavio Bolsonaro leading President Lula, short of a majority, with a runoff on Oct. 25. With 100 percent of polling sections counted early Monday, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party had 56,104,503 votes, 47.03 percent of valid votes, and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party had 53,879,538, 45.16 percent, O Globo reported from Superior Electoral Court data. Augusto Cury was third with 2.89 percent. Neither reached the more than 50 percent of valid votes needed to win outright, so the two meet in a runoff on Oct. 25. Abstention was about 21 percent, the highest since 1998.

Russia launched 205 drones at Ukraine overnight; jet-powered drones killed one person and injured eight in Kharkiv, officials said. Ukraine's Air Force said the attack began at 6 p.m. Sunday Kyiv time and included 49 jet-powered Shahed-type drones; air defenses shot down or suppressed 172 by 8 a.m. Monday, with hits at 13 locations. Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said three Banderol jet drones struck near homes in the Industrialnyi district. Separately, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday the U.S. has proposed technical-level three-way talks with Russia by the end of October and that Ukraine responded positively.

A Merit Systems Protection Board rule ending the required 12-factor review of federal workers' discipline penalties takes effect today. The final rule (Federal Register document 2026-18061, published Sept. 3) replaces the mandatory review of all 12 Douglas factors in misconduct appeals with a test of whether an agency's penalty is reasonable under the totality of the circumstances. It applies to appeals filed on or after Oct. 5; pending appeals stay under the old framework. Individual factors can still be raised, and material mitigating evidence must be considered.

The State Department said it is monitoring a suspected fatal pneumonic plague case in Russia's Irkutsk region with the CDC. A State Department spokesperson told RFE/RL on Oct. 4 that the U.S. is aware of reports of a fatal suspected pneumonic plague case and is monitoring with the CDC and other agencies, and urged Russia to share accurate information quickly and openly; an HHS spokesperson confirmed the CDC is working with State. No new U.S. travel restrictions were announced, and there are no direct commercial flights between the two countries. Russia's Rospotrebnadzor says the 28-year-old Anti-Plague Institute lab technician died of pneumonia of unknown cause, found no work-linked microorganisms in testing, and calls the regional situation stable; about 200 contacts are under observation.

U.S. B-1 bombers used for Iran strikes have left Britain's RAF Fairford and returned home, the Pentagon confirmed. The Pentagon said Sunday that all U.S. bombers deployed to RAF Fairford had re-deployed to their home stations, without saying when they moved or why, and that the bomber force can still strike from the continental United States. The move follows a U.K. counterterrorism investigation near the base: police arrested a 25-year-old British-Iranian man in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, and five U.K. nationals arrested Sept. 27 over suspicious vehicles near the base were released on bail.

Yemen's Saudi-backed government announced a military campaign to retake all territory held by the Iran-backed Houthis. Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Presidential Leadership Council, said in a televised address Sunday that operations would continue until the country is freed from the Houthis, after de-escalation efforts were exhausted; a military spokesman told the Houthis to lay down their weapons. The Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coast, including the Bab al-Mandab Strait, in an offensive last month, and AFP, citing Yemeni military sources, reported they cut the road linking Taiz with Aden on Sunday. The same day, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the group fired missiles and drones at Aramco sites in Riyadh and Khurais; Saudi Arabia had not commented.

France's high-school protests will close up to 500 schools fully or partly Monday, the education minister said; 24 have been burned or ransacked. Education Minister Edouard Geffray said Sunday that lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" at 400 to 500 high schools where security conditions are not met, about the same number as Friday, with a "partial, progressive return" to classes. He said 24 schools have been "burned or ransacked" and 78 education staff injured since the movement began. More than 5,000 people, about 85 percent of them minors, have been arrested. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu sent ministers a roadmap Sunday asking that classes resume wherever safety allows and setting a timetable to answer some student demands, including school renovation talks with regional presidents and Parcoursup proposals by the end of October. In the Paris region, more than 160 of 468 public high schools will be closed Monday, regional president Valerie Pecresse said. A 16-year-old was detained Sunday over Friday's assault on a 59-year-old teacher who was doused with gasoline and struck in La Ciotat. Organizers have called for more protests Tuesday.

Russia's Defense Ministry said it will intensify strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, as drones hit a Kyiv bridge for a fourth straight day. The ministry said the stepped-up attacks on military, defense-industry and related infrastructure respond to President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's vow in a Reuters interview to hit more Russian oil refineries. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were hurt Sunday when a drone struck the Northern Bridge's roadway, a second straight day of hits there. Zelenskiy said a drone killed one person at a Sumy medical-supplies warehouse and six were hurt at a Dnipro communications site; he said Russia fired more than 1,900 drones, 1,700 glide bombs and 25 missiles over the past week. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made an unannounced visit to Kyiv.

Ethiopian government-allied forces entered Mekelle, the Tigray capital, after TPLF rebels announced they had withdrawn following renewed fighting. The Tigray People's Liberation Front said Saturday its forces had pulled out of Mekelle, which they seized along with its airport last month; a witness said government-allied fighters entered the city Sunday. Residents described looting of the TPLF administration office and regional police headquarters as rebel fighters left. Internet and phone outages have made events hard to verify. Ethiopia closed its embassy in Eritrea on Thursday and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats; Eritrea said it was cutting diplomatic ties.

A tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an unknown projectile that damaged its engine room, UKMTO said. UK Maritime Trade Operations Warning 150-26, issued Oct. 4, 2026, says the master of a tanker reported being struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, causing engine-room damage. The crew were reported safe and there was no environmental impact reported at the time. Authorities are investigating. Vessels were advised to transit with caution. The report is distinct from earlier UKMTO warnings on Oct. 1–2 tanker hits in and near Hormuz.

Trump announced a federal AI task force, the "Super Intelligence Force," led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. In a Truth Social post Sunday, the president said the force will coordinate federal engagement with AI companies, consumers, public-interest and religious groups, and infrastructure providers. FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael and OPM Director Scott Kupor will also lead it, reporting to Trump and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. It follows last week's White House meeting where OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia and SpaceXAI signed voluntary safety standards, including internal evaluations, outside audits and board reviews. Trump also named John Coale special presidential envoy for hostage affairs.

A shooting at a block party in Vienna, Georgia, killed two people and injured 35, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation said. The GBI said Dooly County deputies were on patrol at the neighborhood party when shots were fired from the 900 block of Pine Street at about 1:25 a.m. Sunday. Two people were found dead in the 600 block of Pine Street, and victims were taken to several regional hospitals. No arrest has been announced; a $5,000 reward has been offered for information.

item.title: Morning Edition, Sunday, October 4, 2026
item.description:
A tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an unknown projectile that damaged its engine room, UKMTO said. Coast Guard confirms debris from the missing Bermuda–Boston Gulfstream G100 air ambulance off Nantucket; six still missing. The U.S. Coast Guard said Saturday that search crews located a debris field confirmed to be from the Gulfstream G100 medical transport aircraft, tail number C-GRJP, after the FAA reported lost contact about 2 a.m. while the plane flew from Bermuda to Boston. Six people were aboard — four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals — and next of kin have been notified. Assets including HC-144, HC-130, MH-60 and HH-60 aircraft, motor lifeboats from Station Brant Point, and cutter William Sparling have searched about 1,644 square miles over roughly 27 hours. The search remains ongoing; a press conference is set for 11 a.m. Sunday at Coast Guard Base Boston.

USPS competitive shipping prices rise about 6% for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select. Governors' Decision 26-7 sets temporary competitive-product price increases averaging 6.0% for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, USPS Ground Advantage, and Parcel Select. No changes apply to Special Services or International competitive products. Prices take effect 12:00 a.m. CDT Oct. 4, 2026, and roll back to prior approved levels at 12:00 a.m. CST Jan. 17, 2027, unless the Governors act again.

Houthis claimed a missile and drone strike on an Aramco facility near Riyadh; AFP saw fire and smoke there. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Saturday the group targeted an oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones and that the strike sparked fires. An AFP journalist reported flames and smoke rising from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh and saw firefighters working at the Riyadh refinery, with ambulances and police nearby. Saudi authorities and Aramco had not confirmed a successful Houthi strike or damage. Separately, Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV reported 26 Saudi strikes on Sanaa overnight; correspondents in the capital reported hearing explosions and seeing warplanes fire missiles.

Tennessee Corrections Commissioner Frank Strada will resign after the failed lethal injection of Christa Pike. Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday that he accepted Strada's resignation; Strada will leave at the end of October and an interim commissioner will be named later. Strada said the department followed established protocol but that stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as Lee's independent review begins. Pike's attorneys said Friday she remained unconscious and on a ventilator in a Nashville-area hospital after the Sept. 30 attempt, and on Saturday called the resignation justified but said it does nothing to help her now. Lee has already halted Tennessee's remaining scheduled executions for the rest of the year.

The UAE attorney general said the Flydubai co-pilot attacked the captain with a crash axe in an attempted terrorist act. Counsellor Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said Saturday that investigators found the co-pilot on flight FZ1073 began carrying out a plan in the air, striking the captain in the flight deck with a crash axe and trying to take control of the aircraft. The Wednesday flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. He said the inquiry is still establishing motives, any links, and the physical and digital evidence, and that final results will come when that work is done. Flydubai had already said everyone on board was safe and had suspended Tel Aviv flights.

Five Russian air-attack weapons exploded in Moldova after crossing its airspace, President Maia Sandu said. Sandu said Saturday on X that she condemned the morning's attack on Ukraine and that five weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated Moldovan airspace and exploded on its soil. Ukraine's air force said Moscow launched Banderol cruise missiles overnight at the Odesa region, which borders Moldova. In Kyiv, Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said a Russian strike damaged the Northern Bridge's road surface and trolleybus cables and suspended traffic; the Associated Press reported no casualties. Russia's Defense Ministry said it hit the bridge, claiming it is used to move troops and military cargo. Friday's attacks had already forced full or partial closures of three of Kyiv's six road bridges over the Dnipro.

A Gulfstream G100 air ambulance with six people aboard lost contact with the FAA while flying from Bermuda to Boston. The U.S. Coast Guard said the FAA notified its command center early Saturday that controllers had lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 medical transfer aircraft, tail number C-GRJP, traveling from Bermuda to Boston with six people on board. Skyport Bermuda said the Canadian-registered air ambulance departed L.F. Wade International Airport for Boston at about 12:41 a.m. Saturday. Clarence Togeretz, Latitude Air Ambulance's director of flight operations, told CBC News the four crew members — two pilots and two medical staff — are Canadian and that the patient and a relative aboard are not Canadian; Latitude lost contact around 1:30 a.m. as the jet approached Boston. The FAA said it issued a search-and-rescue alert at 1:20 a.m. ET. Coast Guard air and surface crews are searching offshore of Nantucket, including an HC-144 and MH-60 from Air Station Cape Cod, a motor lifeboat crew from Station Brant Point, and the cutter William Sparling. As of Saturday afternoon, no aircraft, wreckage or survivors had been located.

French high-school protests disrupted 735 of about 3,700 schools Friday, with fires at school entrances and 1,747 arrests. The protests began in the Paris region in September and spread nationwide. Students say hours are too long, conditions are poor, including overheated classrooms, and too many staff are absent. Education Minister Edouard Geffray said 735 of about 3,700 schools were affected "in one way or another" on Friday, down 30 percent from Thursday, and that three staff members were injured Friday compared with 31 on Thursday. Since the movement began, he said, at least 65 staff have been injured, including 40 principals, about 170 students have been wounded, and more than 100 high schools have suffered severe damage. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said there were 1,747 arrests on Friday and that more than 300 police officers and gendarmes have been injured. An AFP photographer said fire damaged the entrances of two Paris high schools on Friday. The BBC, citing the regional government, reported more than €2 million in damage at Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes after a fire destroyed its glass entrance and some interior areas. In La Ciotat, officials said a teacher was sprayed with petrol and then assaulted. The Tours prosecutor said a young man injured Wednesday lost the use of his right eye. In Marseille on Thursday, police said hundreds of young people surrounded a fire truck at Saint-Exupery high school, forced the firefighters off it, and set the truck alight, Reuters reported. In Bordeaux on Sept. 29, Gironde prefect Sophie Brocas and academy rector Jean-Marc Huart said a firefighter was injured by an exploding aerosol can, according to press accounts, while putting out a barricade fire near Lycee Montaigne; he was taken to hospital and returned to his station that afternoon with several days off work. Unions and student groups called for further rallies on Tuesday.

A Miami federal judge dismissed a noncitizen-voting case, ruling the federal ban in 18 U.S.C. § 611 is unconstitutional; the Justice Department appealed. U.S. District Judge David S. Leibowitz ruled Thursday that Congress cannot set voter qualifications, a power he said belongs to the states, and dismissed the misdemeanor case against Chelsea Cox. CBS News reported the order applies only to Cox and is the first time a court has held the statute unconstitutional. It does not affect the separate law against false claims of citizenship. The Justice Department moved to appeal.

A crude oil tanker was struck by an unknown projectile four nautical miles east of Oman, the UK maritime office said. UK Maritime Trade Operations warning 149-26 said the master reported a port-side strike at 2142 UTC on Oct. 2. All crew were safe and no environmental impact was reported. Authorities are investigating. The report is separate from Friday morning's strike on an outbound tanker inside the Strait of Hormuz, which UKMTO said caused a small fire and a blackout before that ship continued.

The G7 agreed to a coordinated release of 100 million barrels, including diesel, starting immediately over four months. The leaders' statement, issued Oct. 2 after a virtual meeting, says the release runs through the International Energy Agency and includes a front-loaded substantial diesel release in the first 20 days. Members also agreed not to restrict energy exports to one another and asked the IEA for a follow-up report within 20 days, including on restocking. The statement condemns Iran's attacks and its disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz, and says sanctions on Russia stay in place.

U.S. employers added 29,000 jobs in September and the unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, the Labor Department reported. Nonfarm payrolls rose 29,000, well below economists' roughly 90,000 estimate. Private payrolls gained 46,000 while government employment fell 17,000. July was revised down by 31,000 to a loss of 10,000, and August down by 29,000 to a gain of 133,000 — 60,000 fewer jobs than previously reported for the two months combined. Average hourly earnings rose 3.0% over the year to $37.81. The labor force participation rate was 61.8%.

U.S. stocks closed higher Friday after the soft September jobs report, with the S&P 500 up 0.7% and within 1% of its record. The Associated Press reported the S&P 500 rose 56.27 points to 7,722.72, the Dow rose 250.40 points, or 0.5%, to 51,176.96, and the Nasdaq rose 319.27 points, or 1.2%, to 27,190.86. Traders pared bets that the Federal Reserve will raise rates later this month. For the week the S&P 500 was still down 0.3% and the Dow down 1.3%.

Flydubai halted flights to Tel Aviv after a Dubai–Tel Aviv flight diverted to Saudi Arabia; the airline said all 172 people on board are safe. Chief executive Ghaith Al Ghaith said Friday that everyone on flight FZ1073 is safe and that captain Smit Machchhar is back in the UAE after medical clearance. The Wednesday flight diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Flydubai said it suspended Tel Aviv service until further notice at the authorities' request, and Emirates suspended its codeshare on that route. The UAE attorney general ordered an investigation into the circumstances, motives and any terrorism link. The airline said that investigation should establish what happened on board.

A tanker was struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations office said. UKMTO said the master reported a hit at 1122 GMT during an outbound transit. The strike caused a small fire and a blackout; the fire was extinguished and the vessel continued underway. No casualties or environmental impact were reported. The incident follows Tuesday's strikes on three Liberian-flagged tankers in the same waterway.

CDC declared over a multistate Salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeño peppers that sickened 488 people in 34 states. As of Oct. 2, CDC said the Salmonella Javiana outbreak tied to fresh jalapeños from Sinaloa, Mexico, distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors is over. FDA closed its investigation the same day. Final counts: 488 illnesses, 65 hospitalizations and no deaths; illness onsets ran June 16 to Aug. 26. Traceback pointed to a common grower supplying Coast Citrus; recalled fresh jalapeños are past shelf life, though some longer-shelf products made with them remain on FDA's recall list.

A tanker was struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations office said. UKMTO said the master reported a hit at 1122 GMT during an outbound transit. The strike caused a small fire and a blackout; the fire was extinguished and the vessel continued underway. No casualties or environmental impact were reported. The incident follows Tuesday's strikes on three Liberian-flagged tankers in the same waterway.

Russian aerial attacks forced the partial closure of three Kyiv bridges over the Dnipro River, the capital's mayor said. Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said Russian strikes fully or partly closed three of Kyiv's six road bridges Friday, snarling traffic in what officials described as a new disruption tactic. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 100 drones overnight, including jet-powered models, hitting Kyiv and eight other regions; a drone strike on a Kyiv high-rise killed one person. The European Commission said it disbursed €2.9 billion ($3.3 billion) in the latest financing batch to Ukraine.

item.title: Morning Edition, Friday, October 2, 2026
item.description:
An executive order directs GSA to make America.gov the single online front door for major federal services. Executive Order 14432, signed Sept. 29 and published in the Federal Register on Oct. 2, tells the General Services Administration to run America.gov as a unified, Login.gov-authenticated entry point for public-facing federal services that serve more than 100,000 users a year online. Tax filing and Defense/Intelligence Community services are excluded. OMB has 90 days to issue an implementation memo; agencies must identify covered services and integrate them. In-person, phone, mail and agency sites remain available.

Homeland Security waived New Mexico water laws to speed border-barrier construction in the El Paso Sector. Secretary Markwayne Mullin's determination, effective Oct. 2, waives federal and New Mexico water statutes and related rules for barrier and road work from Border Monument 71 east to Monument 53, north to Monument 40, then east to Monument 1. DHS cited more than 1.24 million Border Patrol apprehensions in the sector from FY2021 through Aug. 30, 2026, and drug seizures including fentanyl. The waiver does not revoke prior Section 102 waivers.

The Pentagon is sending about 9,000 sailors and Marines and a third aircraft carrier toward the Middle East. A U.S. official told AP the move includes the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island amphibious ready group with more than 7,000 sailors and about 2,000 Marines. With forces already there, the Navy presence could exceed 20,000 sailors and Marines and put three carriers in the region by late October. President Trump said new strikes on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterms remain possible and that he rejected Iran's latest ceasefire and Hormuz proposal as inadequate.

Treasury and the IRS issued rules implementing the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit for K-12 school choice. Proposed and companion temporary regulations under IRC §25F (Education Freedom Tax Credit) allow individuals a nonrefundable credit of up to $1,700 a year ($3,400 joint) for cash gifts to eligible Scholarship Granting Organizations in participating states. Contributions may fund private-school tuition, tutoring, special-needs services, books and supplies starting Jan. 1, 2027. Thirty states have opted in; Treasury estimates ~96% of children in those states could be scholarship-eligible and projects up to about 2.2 million scholarships a year by 2030. Temporary rules set state election and SGO certification procedures now; taxpayers may rely on the proposed rules for 2027 contributions.

Federal Medicaid and CHIP funding ended for many refugees, asylees and other legal immigrants. Section 71109 of the 2025 Working Families Tax Cut law took effect Oct. 1, limiting federal Medicaid/CHIP matching funds mainly to U.S. citizens/nationals, lawful permanent residents, Cuban-Haitian entrants and COFA migrants. CMS told states to redetermine affected enrollees; KFF Health News found more than 281,000 people in nine states and D.C. at risk of losing coverage in October, with Florida alone identifying nearly 177,000. Emergency Medicaid for emergency conditions remains; states may still cover lawfully residing children and pregnant women under an existing option. Some states, including California, New York and Pennsylvania, are using state funds to blunt the cut.

Trump Accounts for eligible children begin automatic Treasury enrollment nationwide. Temporary IRS/Treasury regs (TD 10056), effective Sept. 30, say the Secretary will elect on or about Oct. 1, 2026, to create auto accounts for each child who meets age and Social Security-number rules and has no prior election—about 73 million eligible children. Auto accounts accept only Treasury-administered contributions and any $1,000 pilot payment until claimed; families then roll funds to a claimed or other trustee account. Regs also allow approved-class and publicly traded stock general funding contributions.

Treasury began mailing $500 Affordable Care Act refund checks to about 950,000 people in 30 states. The payments go mainly to HealthCare.gov enrollees who paid marketplace user fees and did not get federal premium subsidies, typically people above 400% of the federal poverty level; some unsubsidized people between 100% and 400% also qualify. The 30 states use the federal exchange rather than state-run marketplaces. Texas and Florida have the largest recipient counts. Checks began going out Wednesday with a letter from the president; delivery timing varies.

Cornell agreed to an independent review of its handling of a 2024 fraternity sexual-assault case as prosecutors reopen a charging look. After a September civil lawsuit and public backlash, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office is reexamining the case it declined to charge in 2024. On Thursday the accuser's attorney told NPR she told Cornell police in 2024 she was raped — contradicting the DA's Monday description of her statement; the DA said he had not yet obtained the full interview transcript from the university. Cornell confirmed it will bring in outside counsel for an independent probe, after Gov. Kathy Hochul called for a review. The university also edited a public FAQ that had said campus police shared all investigatory information with the DA's office.

A ~50-vehicle pileup on southbound I-95 over Lake Marion closed the corridor in South Carolina for an extended period. The morning crash near mile marker 100 on the Orangeburg/Clarendon County line involved about 50 vehicles, including roughly 15 tractor-trailers, South Carolina Highway Patrol and local outlets said. Dense fog was reported. About 11 people were hospitalized with minor injuries; the Clarendon County coroner said there were no deaths. Northbound lanes later reopened with slow traffic; southbound lanes stayed closed while crews cleared the bridge, with an SCDOT detour at mile marker 102. Officials urged drivers to avoid the area.

Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan's Helmand and Kunar provinces killed at least 10 civilians, Afghanistan and the U.N. said. The U.N. mission in Afghanistan said most of the dead were children and nine people were wounded. Pakistan's information ministry said the overnight strikes hit militant hideouts and that initial reports suggested 22 militants were killed; it did not immediately address civilian casualty reports. Afghanistan's Taliban government called the raids an act of aggression. The neighbors have traded cross-border fire for months over Pakistan's claims that militants operate from Afghan soil.

item.title: Morning Edition, Thursday, October 1, 2026
item.description:
Tennessee halted scheduled executions after Christa Pike appeared still breathing following a lethal injection attempt. Witnesses said Pike still appeared to be breathing about an hour after pentobarbital was administered late Wednesday at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville; she was taken to a hospital. Gov. Bill Lee ordered a third-party review and said the remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year. Earlier Wednesday the Supreme Court vacated a Sixth Circuit stay (Nelsen v. Pike, 26A428), clearing Tennessee to proceed before the warrant expired at midnight; Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson dissented. Pike, 50, was convicted of the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer and was the only woman on Tennessee's death row.

A State Department rule removed Syria from the blanket ban on U.S. defense-trade licenses. The International Traffic in Arms Regulations final rule, effective Oct. 1, takes Syria off ITAR §126.1's list of countries subject to a policy of denial for defense exports and imports. License requests will be reviewed case by case. The change follows the secretary's Aug. 19 defense-trade policy shift after statutory barriers, including terrorism-related restrictions, were lifted or waived. Belarus, Burma, China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Venezuela remain on the denial list.

USDA rewrote Rural Energy for America grants so projects must already be built before applicants can apply. The Rural Business-Cooperative Service final rule, published Oct. 1 and effective Oct. 16, shifts REAP renewable-energy and efficiency grants to a post-completion model using 12 months of actual performance data. It bars solar and wind systems on Farm Service Agency–certified cropland, bars components from foreign-adversary countries, limits applicants to highest-level owners, and replaces state contests with national scoring. Comments are due Nov. 2.

The Yankees, Padres and White Sox each swept their MLB Wild Card Series; the Phillies forced a Game 3. On Wednesday the Yankees beat the Red Sox 9-2, the White Sox beat the Astros 7-3 and the Padres beat the Cubs 4-1 to advance to the Division Series. The Phillies beat the Braves 4-3 in 10 innings, forcing a decisive Game 3 on Thursday.

The Senate confirmed Keith Sonderling as Labor secretary. The nomination was confirmed 47-41 on a party-line vote late Wednesday (roll call 256), with 12 senators not voting. Sonderling had been serving as acting labor secretary. The vote came after the Senate earlier Wednesday invoked cloture on the nomination 53-47.

The United States ended its anti-ISIS military mission in Iraq, withdrawing the last U.S. troops after more than two decades. Operation Inherent Resolve's Iraq mission concluded Wednesday under a 2024 Baghdad-Washington transition plan; roughly 2,500 remaining U.S. forces left, with Iraq assuming full responsibility for security against ISIS remnants. Iran and aligned groups cast the exit as a win. The U.S. and Iraq say they will shift to a bilateral security relationship; concerns remain about militia influence and residual ISIS threats without U.S. air and intelligence support on the ground.

A Flydubai pilot stabbed the other pilot on a Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight and apparently tried to crash the plane, Israel's prime minister said. Flight FZ1073 (Dubai to Tel Aviv) transmitted emergency codes including 7500 (unlawful interference), descended thousands of feet, and diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia; Israel scrambled warplanes amid hijacking fears. Netanyahu said one pilot stabbed the other and apparently tried to crash the Boeing 737; Flydubai confirmed a flight-deck altercation, said all passengers were safe, and said motives remain under investigation. Saudi airport officials said both pilots were hospitalized; Saudi and UAE authorities opened investigations.

Iran received a formal U.S. response to its proposal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented the U.S. response to President Masoud Pezeshkian at Wednesday's cabinet meeting after receiving feedback via Qatari mediators in Doha on Tuesday night, officials said. The contents were not disclosed. A Reuters-briefed official said the main disagreement is the sequencing of a seven-day trust-building plan, not its components. President Trump had publicly rejected Iran's earlier offer days ago; mediators kept working. Pezeshkian said Iran would seek a "win-win" agreement.

The Ratepayer Protection Act and the Stop Insider Trading Act, both House-passed bills, failed in the Senate. Both needed 60 votes to advance and fell short the same afternoon. The Ratepayer Protection Act (vote 254, 57-43) would have pushed state utility regulators to keep large data-center power and water costs off residential ratepayers; four Democrats — Hassan, Klobuchar, Ossoff and Warnock — joined Republicans; the House had passed it 417-3. The Stop Insider Trading Act (vote 253, 53-47, party-line) would have barred members, spouses and dependent children from buying new publicly traded stocks while allowing sales with advance notice and letting them keep existing holdings. Separately, the Senate voted 53-47 to invoke cloture on Keith Sonderling’s nomination as Labor secretary (vote 255), clearing a procedural step toward a final confirmation vote.

Russian strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight killed four people, including a child, and hit power infrastructure. President Zelenskyy said the main targets were energy infrastructure in Kyiv and the surrounding region. The Russian Defense Ministry claimed hits on a hydroelectric plant, a thermal plant, a substation, an energy storage facility and a data center; Ukrainian officials did not confirm those specific targets and reported hits on civilian areas in at least four Kyiv districts. Ukraine's air force said Russia is using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones that are hard to intercept.

Armada Acquisition Corp. II shareholders approved the Evernorth XRP-treasury merger, a step toward a planned Nasdaq listing as XRPN. The noon-ET special meeting cleared the business-combination vote, according to meeting attendees reported by crypto.news; an official SEC 8-K with final tallies had not posted by evening research. Proxy materials project at least about 473 million XRP at closing if the deal closes. Approval is not the same as listing or trading — remaining closing conditions and Nasdaq requirements still apply, with completion targeted for late 2026.

OFAC published a final rule putting 2020 Iran sector sanctions into the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations, effective Sept. 30. The rule amends 31 CFR part 560 to implement Executive Order 13902, which authorizes blocking of persons operating in Iran's construction, mining, manufacturing or textiles sectors, among other authorities, and adds humanitarian and U.N. official-business exemptions. OFAC has already used E.O. 13902 for designations; this updates the Code of Federal Regulations. Willful violations may carry criminal penalties under IEEPA.

The Yankees, Braves, Padres and White Sox each won Game 1 of their MLB Wild Card Series on Tuesday. Yankees beat the Red Sox 9-0; Braves beat the Phillies 5-3; Padres beat the Cubs 8-0; White Sox beat the Astros 6-3. All four series are best-of-three; Game 2s are Wednesday. Teams that take a 1-0 lead have historically won the Wild Card Series about 88% of the time.

The Senate rejected, 47-51, a motion to force a floor vote on a resolution seeking a State Department report on Israel's human rights record. The motion would have discharged S.Res. 852, sponsored by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, from the Foreign Relations Committee under Section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act. Sen. Rand Paul was the only Republican voting yes; Sen. John Fetterman was the only Democrat voting no. Sens. Cassidy and Sullivan did not vote. The Senate adjourned at 8:15 p.m.

The Transportation Department finalized lower fuel economy standards for new cars and light trucks. New vehicles must average 34.9 miles per gallon by model year 2031, down from about 50 mpg under the previous rules. The rule covers model years 2022 through 2031, ends the credit-trading program automakers use to meet the standards starting in 2028, and changes how vehicles are classified as cars or light trucks in 2030. The department estimates it lowers the average new-vehicle price by about $1,300. Environmental groups criticized the change.

A 100% Section 232 tariff on most patented drug imports took effect for companies not covered by the July phase-in. Under Proclamation 11020, the additional duties applied to Annex III companies from July 31 and to all other companies' patented pharmaceuticals and ingredients entered on or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern on Sept. 29. Rates range from 0% to 100% depending on patent status, country, onshoring agreements and use; generics and many U.S.-origin products are excluded. Partner jurisdictions such as the U.K. can face 0%, and EU/Japan/South Korea/Switzerland/Liechtenstein patented articles face 15%.

The Supreme Court let the administration resume deporting immigrants to countries other than their own while the case continues. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson would have denied the request. The order pauses a Massachusetts federal judge's ruling, upheld by the 1st Circuit, that the policy denied immigrants a chance to raise fears of torture or persecution in the destination country. Deportations have included flights to El Salvador, Libya and South Sudan. The court will hear arguments in December, with a decision expected by summer 2027.

The Energy Department offered to exchange up to 40 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The request for proposal is the final tranche of the United States' 172-million-barrel contribution to a coordinated International Energy Agency release of about 400 million barrels after Middle East supply disruption. Crude would come from the Big Hill and Bryan Mound sites, with deliveries scheduled for November and December 2026; companies must return the oil plus premium barrels. Bids are due Oct. 6. Energy Secretary Chris Wright urged European countries to fulfill their release pledges.

Treasury sanctioned 10 people and companies it says procured weapons for Iran's Defense Ministry. Under Operation Economic Outcast, OFAC designated individuals and entities in Iran, Hong Kong, China, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey tied to procurement for Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics, including networks supplying electronics for drones and ballistic missiles. The action was taken under E.O. 13382. U.S.-linked assets of the designated persons are blocked.

item.title: Evening Edition, Tuesday, September 29, 2026
item.description:
The Education Department finalized a rule rescinding the Biden administration's 2024 Title IX regulations and restoring the 2020 rules; it was announced Sept. 28 and published Sept. 29. The 2024 rule, which had added gender identity protections and changed sexual misconduct procedures, was already struck down by a federal court. The restored rules govern how schools and colleges receiving federal funds investigate sexual harassment and misconduct complaints. Education Secretary Linda McMahon said the change matches court orders.

U.S. bans on imports of Canadian-bottled wine and spirits, whey and some motorcycles took effect at 12:01 a.m. Eastern on Sept. 29 under executive orders signed by President Trump. The banned goods totaled about $967 million in 2025 imports, and alcohol makes up 87% of that. The orders target Canadian provinces that pulled U.S. alcohol from store shelves. U.S.-Canada trade talks broke down in August; Ontario announced $1.15 billion in financing for affected businesses.

The Senate passed the Protect College Sports Act 77-22 on Sept. 28. The bill creates a federal right for college athletes to be paid for their name, image and likeness, requires schools to share media, ticket and sponsorship revenue, caps agent fees at 5%, and guarantees medical coverage for five years after eligibility ends. It now goes to the House.

item.title: Morning Edition, Tuesday, September 29, 2026
item.description:
President Trump rejected Iran's latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the war. Iran had offered terms to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil shipments, and end the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, now in its seventh month. Iran's foreign minister said Iran will wait for a formal U.S. response before abandoning ceasefire talks. Eight U.S. Marines were injured by an Iranian missile in the strait on Sept. 14.

The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.2% on Sept. 28, its highest level in 19 years, and U.S. crude oil rose 4.2% to $96.31 a barrel after President Trump rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. All three major stock indexes closed lower: the S&P 500 fell 0.77% to 7,683.69, the Dow 0.67% and the Nasdaq 0.92%. Brent crude briefly traded above $108 before settling near $98. The 10-year yield is a benchmark for mortgage and other long-term loan rates.

President Trump announced at 2:00 p.m. that Mesabi Metallics, owned by India-based Essar Group, plans a $15 billion steel mill in eastern Iowa, using ore from its mine near Nashwauk, Minnesota. The mill would use iron ore from Mesabi Metallics' new mine near Nashwauk on Minnesota's Iron Range, which opened this month; the mine has hired over 200 of a planned 350 workers. Mesabi Metallics is owned by India-based Essar Group. No construction start date or mill job count was given.

Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi said Iran is waiting for an official U.S. response before ending ceasefire talks; an Iranian official said Iran will not change its position on its nuclear program. The statements followed the U.S. rejection of Iran's proposal. An Iranian army spokesman also said Iran's forces are prepared for renewed U.S. attacks.

SpaceX's Starship reached orbit for the first time on its 14th test flight Monday, deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites. The ship completed about six orbits over roughly 10 hours before splashing down in the Pacific west of Chile; the Super Heavy booster splashed down in the Gulf shortly after launch. SpaceX changed the booster after ice buildup caused problems on the previous flight. NASA plans to use a modified Starship as the moon lander for its Artemis program.
